There comes a time in every avid reader’s life when they must put away serious things and take up more (im)mature ones. Rebecca Yarros’ Fourth Wing was the first novel to shift my perspective on the BookTok-dubbed genre of ‘romantasy’. While I’m not hailing it as a piece of prized literature, I can safely declare it to be an enthralling book with well-developed characters and the perfect balance of romance and fantasy. Chances are you agree, or else you wouldn’t have landed on this article. Yarros’ latest instalment, Threshing Day , was released on 29 September – and if you’ve already torn through its 13 stories, you’re in the right place. Read more: New Fourth Wing book, Threshing Day, has landed with 50% off There’s something inherently healing about loosening one’s grasp on high literature and delving into the murky depths of high fantasy and romance instead. This isn’t to say that some novels which fall within the genre are not, or cannot be, considered high-brow classics – far from it.

Beyond plotting, betrayal, and cold-blooded murder, the rugged, romantic Scottish landscape steals the show in The Traitors. Filmed at Ardross Castle, the privately owned historic property is as much a main character as presenter Claudia Winkleman ( and her coat collection ). Built in the Scottish Baronial style, the 19th-century estate is spread across 100 acres of parkland, north of Inverness along the River Alness. Its imposing facade, grand staircases and turrets set the moody tone of the TV show. Beyond the castle, shots of misty glens, brooding skies and forest wildernesses have increasingly put Scotland on the tourism map. Since the first series of The Traitors aired in 2022, the show has delivered an estimated £21.8 million boost to the Scottish economy, according to the BBC’s economic impact report.

Earlier this year, Manchester Airport showcased a selection of items its security officers were forced to confiscate in the space of just one morning. CASES of aggressive bowel cancer that kills half of those it strikes are rising in teens and young adults, scientists warn. As the disease historically affects older adults, youngsters may be missing warning signs – which include tummy aches and lower back pain. Researchers from Mass General Brigham for Children and Mass General Brigham Cancer Institute found that children and teens with bowel cancer face “extreme delays” in diagnosis. As a result, many won’t be diagnosed with cancer until it’s reached an advanced stage – making treatment trickier and increasing the likelihood of death. FOR the millions of Brits with ADHD, a daily stimulant tablet holds the potential to unlock a new world – one that is quieter, less chaotic, with a level playing field. The surge in prescription drugs for ADHD has been explosive in the past few years. But for some, it’s not all it’s cracked up to be. Others are spooked by little-known risks on the heart and even death, leaving them searching more desperately for answers to manage symptoms. When Michelle Akpata, 30, was diagnosed with ADHD, she hoped a prescription from her GP would rid her of the extra load she’d been carrying for years. “It often felt like running a marathon mentally just to stay organised throughout the day,” says Michelle, a broadcaster and radio presenter from London . “I realised that my difficulty maintaining focus and structure wasn’t just stress, but a consistent pattern affecting my day-to-day life.” But after starting Ritalin (10mg), the initial surge in energy gave way to troubling side effects.

items.text: The truth behind your menopause supplements: How the health industry is preying on midlife women with HRT alternatives, exposed by doctor and broadcaster XAND VAN TULLEKEN
items.article: Are you a woman worried about the menopause? There's a supplement for that. Dozens, in fact - as well as menopause shampoo, menopause face cream and even menopause chocolate. Published: 01:00, 7 September 2026 | Updated: 09:24, 7 September 2026 Dr Xand van Tulleken previously exposed the truth about celebrity-endorsed supplements that claim to promote longevity . Now, he delves into the booming menopause industry and reveals the damaging role social media plays in the promotion of wellness. Are you a woman worried about the menopause ? There’s a supplement for that. Dozens, in fact – as well as menopause shampoo, menopause face cream, menopause clothes… and even menopause chocolate. How did the menopause create such a booming industry? The answer goes back almost a quarter of a century to 2002, when part of a major HRT trial was stopped early. The headline finding was a 26 per cent increase in invasive breast cancer in the women taking combined oestrogen and progestin – the standard HRT – compared with those on placebo. The trial had also found increases in heart attack, stroke and blood clots, partly offset by fewer hip fractures and cases of colon cancer. The study was later found to be flawed – the actual increased risk was a tiny 0.5 per cent – but it kick-started a major panic among women with the result that many either stopped taking HRT or decided to avoid it altogether.
